newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Meyer says SNB should aim for long-term stability.
newsitem.headline: Meyer says SNB should aim for long-term stability.

text.p: Swiss National Bank Chairman Hans Meyer said he favoured monetary policy which provides flexibility in the short-run but has central aim of achieving long-term price stability.
He said the central bank believed any monetary policy tools should be used with restraint.

"A careful monetary policy maker avoids economic policy activism. He has no other choice than to take a long view. His highest goal consists of avoiding gross errors, and through that, to keep inflation under control long-term," Meyer said in the text of a speech to be delivered to an economic forum.
"In contrast, he cannot ever completely control economic ups and downs. Trying to do more places too great a demand on monetary policy and holds the danger of destabilising the economy," Meyer said.
He noted that in Switzerland it may take three years before a change in monetary policy affects price levels.
He also said the SNB's most recent discount rate cut on September 26 to 1.00 percent from 1.50 percent underscored its desire to smooth out money market turbulence.
Meyer made no reference to currency markets, where the Swiss franc has lately weakened, focusing instead on domestic policy.
But he also took pains to explain that tightness in the Swiss money market earlier this year was linked to technical factors rather than any SNB policy change.
"It was clear from our comments (at a June press conference) that there was no monetary policy necessity for a rate rise," he said.
He reiterated that recent shifts in domestic bank holdings to SNB sight deposits and out of postal accounts had caused tightness in the money market, contrary to what the SNB wanted.

"We made clear that this liquidity tightness was unwanted. As a consequence, money market rates fell again and returned to levels seen in spring 1996. We underscored our efforts to smooth the waves in the money market with our discount rate cut to 1.00 percent from 1.50 percent," Meyer said.
He expected distortions in money aggregates stemming from deposit shifts to be temporary, and reaffirmed the validity of using a monetary aggregate target to guide policy longer-term.

"We can regard the close connection between money supply growth and the inflation rate as a macro-economic natural law," Meyer said. The SNB's medium-term growth path for its money aggregate was its policy "anchor."
"But, on a short- or medium-term basis, we allow -- when necessary -- significant deviations from the central bank target path," he said, adding that monetary control must be tempered with reason.
"Instead of following mechanical rules, we trust economic analysis and healthy human judgement," Meyer said.
He did not rule out some adjustments to the target itself if the money supply aggregate showed significant distortions.

"We have done well by following this strategy in the past and believe that this will remain so in the foreseeable future. But that does not exclude adjusting our monetary policy strategy in the future, to the extent that the target path for the central bank money aggregate proves to be inadequate because of significant changes in relationships," Meyer said.
"We are not dogmatic. The aforementioned intention is no ideology for us, but rather a means to an end, (which is) to keep inflation under control as much as we can," Meyer said.
